title: Traffic replay stitching and occupancy capture
content:
Purpose:
This doc captures a lightweight, repeatable method for constructing long-duration throughput runs by stitching together many shorter recorded traces. The goal is to produce occupancy-stable runs (steady windows) that are reproducible across hardware and software revisions while avoiding long single-shot recordings (which are brittle and expensive to iterate).

Summary / high level:
- Record short client traces from real traffic or synthetic generators (30s–3min). Annotate with monotonic timestamps and request metadata (sequence length, token counts, model, route).
- Normalize traces to a canonical event format and RNG-seed them when sampling synthetic variants.
- Stitch traces into a continuous timeline using controlled inter-trace gaps and a jitter filter to avoid accidental synchrony.
- Run final replay under three-phase schedule: cold soak, ramp, steady-window capture. Capture raw traces, system metrics and kernel-level breakdowns.

Why this approach?
- Short recordings are easier to collect, label, and sanitize for PII.
- Stitching allows many experiments to reuse the same corpus but vary seeds, inter-arrival jitter, and concurrency without re-recording customer traffic.
- Controlled gaps + jitter reduce microburst artifacts caused by aligning many sources.

Key definitions (how we use terms):
- trace: a time-ordered sequence of client request events from a single client or session.
- stitch-run: a synthetic continuous run built by concatenating traces with controlled timing adjustments.
- occupancy window: a contiguous interval where request arrival rate and service backlog are statistically stable (used for throughput assertions).
- priming: prefix or request sequences sent before measured window to warm caches, kernel states, and KV caches.

Step-by-step recipe (practical):
1) Collection: gather 30–90s traces from representative clients. Include these fields per event: monotonic_ts (ns), client_id, request_id, model, seq_len, token_count, seed (if synthetic), raw_prompt_hash. Keep each trace as separate file.

2) Normalization: convert timestamps to relative (0..T) and add a normalized inter-arrival target (events/sec). Optionally bucket by seq_len percentiles.

3) Trace selection policy: for a run pick N traces from the corpus using a sampler (weighted by client weight). Use deterministic sampler with explicit seed to ensure repeatability. Record the sampler seed in run metadata.

4) Stitching algorithm (simple deterministic):
   - sort selected traces by original client_id (or shuffle using sampler seed).
   - set an inter-trace gap G: choose from {10ms, 50ms, 200ms} depending on desired burstiness.
   - for each trace i, offset all events by cumulative_offset + i*G + jitter_i where jitter_i ~ Uniform(-g/2,g/2) and g = min(0.2*G, 5ms).
   - after offsetting, re-calculate global arrival process and apply a low-pass filter: if >K events fall into a 1ms window (K=limit per test), spread them evenly over that ms to avoid kernel enqueue spikes.
   - output: single event timeline file with monotonic timestamps suitable for the loadgen player.

5) Clock sync and player coordination:
   - use a monotonic clock on clients (CLOCK_MONOTONIC_RAW). Do not rely on wall clock across different machines.
   - players must be started with an agreed start-offset and aligned by an initial handshake message. Use a simple RPC to negotiate start_time = now + Xs. Avoid NTP during tests; instead use the handshake to align local monotonic baselines.
   - embed per-event relative times; loadgen players should use local monotonic start and schedule sends precisely.

6) Warmup schedule and capture windows:
   - cold soak: 120–300s at low QPS (10–20% target) to allow thermal drift and network reconnections.
   - ramp: 60–180s linearly ramp to target QPS.
   - steady capture: 300–1800s capture window (choose longer for multi-tenant variance). Only compute throughput numbers from the central steady window (trim first/last 10%).

7) Metrics to capture (minimum):
   - per-request: request latency (wall and server processing), token_count, model version, route id, queue_wait_time
   - system: GPU utilization, GPU memory, SM active, temperature, CPU load by service process, network transmit/recv, PCIe counters
   - runtime internals: scheduler queue lengths, batch sizes, KV cache hit/miss, kernel durations (attention, matmul, softmax)
   - observability: request ids tracing to correlate traces and server logs (trace_id header)

Repeatability checklist (must pass before an official run):
- corpus seed recorded and checked-in to run metadata; sampler seed logged
- players verified to use CLOCK_MONOTONIC_RAW and handshake alignment passed
- node provisioning consistent: same GPU firmware, driver, CUDA/CuBLAS/Kernel versions logged
- ambient thermal stable: GPUs preconditioned for >30min unless testing cold-start
- model weights/quantization profile pinned and checksumed
- network QoS identical (same VPC/subnet rules)
- randomization knobs (jitter, gap) recorded and immutable for the run

Loadgen example snippet (player config - plain format):
start-offset: 10s
sampler-seed: 934201
selected-traces: 120
inter-trace-gap-ms: 50
jitter-ms: 5
player-mode: scheduled
clock-source: CLOCK_MONOTONIC_RAW

Warmup tuning notes / heuristics:
- If first 60s of steady window shows >5% downward slope in throughput -> increase ramp length.
- If P99 latency > target with GPU idle cycles visible -> suspect kernel scheduling / batch packing mismatch. Capture kernel trace.
- Use a micro-observation run (2x shorter) to validate stitch quality before expensive long runs.

Troubleshooting (common flakes):
- Symptom: sudden 100ms spikes at predictable offsets -> likely multiple traces aligning; fix: increase inter-trace-G and jitter.
- Symptom: lower-than-expected throughput with high CPU -> player-side bottleneck; inspect client send loop and network buffers.
- Symptom: inconsistent results across runs -> check seeds, driver versions, thermal history. Re-run with preconditioned GPUs.

Open questions / TODOs:
- Evaluate adaptive gap selection: algorithm that picks G per trace pair based on sequence-length mix to minimize enqueue pressure.
- Automate corpus sanitization to strip PII in recorded prompts while preserving seq_len distribution.
- Add a lightweight checksum for event timelines so we can assert the stitched output is bit-identical when seeds and sampling are the same.

Quick checklist for someone running this doc for the first time:
- [ ] checkout corpus repo (linked artifacts) and validate sample counts
- [ ] pick sampler-seed and document it in JIRA-SRV-8421
- [ ] run micro-observation (3min) and validate jitter/gap params
- [ ] run full warmup+capture and upload run metadata + kernel traces to S3 path

Notes to self: keep captures small when iterating. aim for 5–10 micro-observations before a full 30–60min assertion run.

Comments welcome: ping @marco or @chen on #bench-harness when you run into odd alignment issues.
